Description: Located in the Madanpur block, Madneshwar Dham is a highly revered ancient Shiva temple and the spiritual heart of Araria. It features a unique Shivalinga and a large sacred pond, drawing thousands during Shravani Mela. Historically, it is a key landmark in the Mithila-Seemanchal cultural belt.

This serene temple near the Sone River serves as a vital center for Buddhist spiritualism and meditation in Arwal. The temple architecture and golden Buddha statue make it a tranquil destination for pilgrims and moral educators.

A 15th-century stone architectural marvel, this unique Sun temple famously faces west. It is the primary site for the Chhath festival in south Bihar, showcasing the engineering prowess of the Nagara style with its massive, mortar-less stone blocks.

A 700-foot granite hill famous for the Samudra Manthan legend. It houses significant rock-cut sculptures and both Hindu and Jain temples at the summit. Geographically, it is a prominent monadnock offering panoramic views of the Banka region.

Asia's largest freshwater oxbow lake and Bihar's first Ramsar site. It is a critical wintering ground for over 60 species of migratory birds from Siberia. It is a major hydrological marker for the Gandak-Burhi Gandak floodplains.

Founded by King Dharmapala, this ancient university was a global hub for Vajrayana Buddhism. The ruins include a massive cruciform stupa and monastic cells, standing as a testament to Bihar's intellectual and educational heritage on the banks of the Ganga.

The ancestral home of 1857 hero Babu Veer Kunwar Singh. The fort is a symbol of Indian resistance against British rule and houses a museum dedicated to the First War of Independence. It is a major socio-political landmark in western Bihar.

The site of the historic 1539 battle where Sher Shah Suri defeated Emperor Humayun. Located at the confluence of the Karmanasa and Ganga, it is an essential monitoring point for river water levels and historical-military research.

A magnificent red-brick fort complex showcasing Mughal-Rajput-European architecture. Home to the Shyama Mai temple and beautiful palaces, it represents the cultural and royal legacy of the Mithila region and the Darbhanga Raj.

The world's largest Buddhist stupa, standing at 104 feet. Built by Ashoka and the Guptas, it commemorates the site where Buddha gave his alms bowl to the people of Vaishali. It is a primary landmark for the Buddhist Circuit and Gandak basin weather.

A UNESCO World Heritage site where Siddhartha Gautama attained Enlightenment. The complex includes the Bodhi Tree and the grand 5th-century brick temple. It is the most sacred destination for Buddhists and a global tourism hub.

A revered Shakti Peeth located in a dense forest pocket. Famous for the legend of 'Thawe Wali Maa,' it draws massive crowds during Navratri. The forest provides a unique micro-climate in the northwestern plains of Bihar.

Built in 1909 to commemorate Lord Minto’s visit, this clock tower is a symbol of the Gidhaur Raj. It stands in a rugged, hilly terrain on the edge of the plateau, serving as a primary marker for south Bihar's highland weather.

The oldest surviving rock-cut caves in India (3rd Century BCE). Known for their mirror-like interior polish and acoustic resonance, they are Mauryan architectural marvels carved out of massive granite monoliths.

Located atop Piwara hill, this is the oldest functional Hindu temple in India (c. 635 CE). It offers commanding views of the Kaimur plateau and is a vital altitude-based observation point for southern weather patterns.

Bihar's first Community Reserve and a critical oxbow lake wetland. It is a sanctuary for hundreds of bird species and a key indicator for the hydrological health of the Mahananda-Ganga river system in eastern Bihar.
A major Shakti Peeth located at a complex river confluence. It is a sentinel for monitoring the high humidity and multi-river flood patterns typical of Khagaria's unique river-heavy geography.

The only tea-producing region in Bihar, benefiting from high rainfall and acidic soil. These lush gardens mark the wettest and most humid part of the state, serving as an early indicator for the arrival of the southwest monsoon.
Famous for a massive Shivalinga discovered in 1977, this grand complex is a premier pilgrimage center. It anchors the cultural identity of the Kiul river basin and the historical Pala empire region.
A legendary Shiva temple associated with King Dasharatha's yajna. It is the focal point of the massive Shravani Mela and a primary landmark for monitoring the weather in the Kosi river belt.

Exquisite ruins of 20th-century Mithila architecture featuring the ornate Kali Temple. Historically a hub for Mithila art and Darbhanga Raj history, it is a key landmark for the Indo-Nepal border plains.

Perched on the Ganga, this fort houses the Bihar School of Yoga and ancient step-wells. Historically the capital of Mir Qasim, it is a critical station for monitoring the Ganga's flow and humidity at the rocky river bend.
A perfectly preserved Ashokan pillar topped by a lion. Historically part of the Lichchavi Republic, it is a vital topographical marker for the fertile, lichi-growing Gandak basin plains.
A white marble pagoda atop Ratnagiri Hill symbolizing global harmony. Accessible by ropeway, it is a high-altitude observation point for wind currents and regional visibility in the Rajgir hills.
The 'Niagara of Bihar,' a 160-foot natural cascade with ice-cold water. It is a major eco-tourism site and a critical point for monitoring flash floods and hill-stream surges in the southern hills.

A beehive-shaped colonial granary built after the 1770 famine. Standing near the Ganga, it is Patna’s most iconic landmark and a key site for monitoring urban heat island effects and riverside weather.
A significant mythological site linked to Lord Narasimha. Historically a regional administrative center, it marks the jute-growing belt and the high-rainfall transition zone of northeast Bihar.

A UNESCO World Heritage octagonal tomb floating in an artificial lake. Often called the 'Second Taj Mahal,' it represents the architectural peak of the Indo-Islamic style and anchors south Bihar’s plains.
A sacred Shakti Peeth and the site of the debate between Adi Shankaracharya and Mandana Misra. It is a sentinel landmark for monitoring the Kosi embankments and river safety.

A premier agricultural university and the birthplace of the Green Revolution in India. It houses the most important meteorological observatory in Bihar, providing foundational data for the entire state.
Situated at the Ganga-Gandak confluence, it is the home of Asia’s largest cattle fair. It is a primary station for monitoring river mist and wind patterns at Bihar's central river corridor.
Features one of the world's largest Vishnu idols discovered in the 1990s. It is a key central Bihar landmark for monitoring soil moisture and the semi-arid climate of the southern plains.
An ancient Shiva temple near the Bagmati embankment, believed to date to the Dwapara Yuga. It is the primary reference point for assessing flood risks in Bihar's smallest district.
Revered as the birthplace of Goddess Sita, featuring the Janaki Kund. It is a vital pilgrimage hub and a key point for monitoring the Indo-Nepal border weather and Lakhandei river levels.
The ancestral home of India’s first President, maintained as a national monument. It is a primary socio-cultural landmark.
A massive hydrological structure with 56 gates regulating the Kosi River. It is the cornerstone of Bihar's flood forecasting system and a critical landmark for monitoring river discharge from Nepal.
An ancient coronation tank of the world’s first republic. It serves as a local temperature stabilizer and a marker for the humidity-rich climate of the Gandak-Ganga interfluve.
Bihar's only National Park, situated at the Himalayan foothills. It is a critical observation point for mountain-influenced weather systems, forest fire risks, and Gandak river discharge.
